title: Chandrasekaran Resigns as Tata Sons Chairman After Six-Month Feud With Noel Tata
excerpt: The departure triggers a selloff across Tata Group stocks, with TCS down 5.1%, as the 158-year-old conglomerate faces its latest leadership crisis.
body:
• N. Chandrasekaran has resigned as Tata Sons chairman after a six-month standoff with Tata Trusts chairman Noel Tata over his reappointment.
  • TCS shares dropped 5.1%, Tata Motors fell 2.5%, and Tata Steel and Titan each lost about 2% following the announcement.
  • Key disagreements centered on whether to list Tata Sons publicly, Air India losses, and board representation.
  • Chandrasekaran will serve out his current term ending in February 2027, giving the $185 billion conglomerate time to find a successor.

N. Chandrasekaran, the chairman of India's Tata Sons, announced his resignation on Wednesday after months of unresolved tensions with the Tata Trusts, the charitable arm that holds a controlling 66% stake in the conglomerate's holding company.

In a statement, Chandrasekaran said he would not seek reappointment at the end of his current term but would continue in the role until February. "It has been 6 months since that board meeting, and no resolution has been reached till date," he said, referring to a February meeting at which Tata Trusts chairman Noel Tata opposed his reappointment.

"Tata Sons is a very large institution and there are many strategic projects that are under critical stages of execution ... clarity on leadership is important for employees, investors, partners and other stakeholders."

— N. Chandrasekaran, outgoing Tata Sons Chairman

Markets React Sharply

The Sensex fell sharply as Tata Group stocks extended their losses through Wednesday's trading session. TCS, where Chandrasekaran built his entire corporate career, led the decline with a 5.1% slide. Jaguar Land Rover parent Tata Motors dropped 2.5%, while Tata Steel and jewelry-to-watches brand Titan each fell roughly 2%.

The selloff underscored the outsized influence of leadership stability on investor sentiment across a conglomerate with 26 listed companies and a combined market capitalization of $277 billion as of March 31, according to Reuters.

A Rift Months in the Making

The disagreements between Chandrasekaran, 63, and Noel Tata had been building over several fronts. The two clashed over whether Tata Sons should pursue a public listing, how to manage losses at Air India — the airline marred by a fatal crash that killed over 240 people in June 2025 — the planned exit of a minority shareholder, and board composition.

A source with direct knowledge of the decision told Reuters the feud with Tata Trusts was the sole reason for Chandrasekaran's resignation. Tata Trusts did not respond to Reuters' request for comment.

The power struggle echoes a 2016 episode when Tata Sons' board sacked its then-chairman Cyrus Mistry after he clashed with the late Ratan Tata, who led the Tata Trusts at the time, over corporate governance. Internal feuds between Tata Sons and Tata Trusts have periodically roiled the 158-year-old institution.

Chandrasekaran's Legacy

Chandrasekaran joined the Tata Group in 1987 as an intern at TCS and rose through the ranks to become the IT firm's CEO in 2009 before being elevated to Tata Sons chairman in 2017. Under his watch, the conglomerate navigated TCS's expansion into a $30 billion revenue company, acquired Air India back from the government, and managed the fallout from regulatory scrutiny and a cyberattack at Jaguar Land Rover that disrupted British manufacturing output.

In the past financial year, Tata Group companies recorded combined revenue of $185 billion, with the group's reach extending from salt and pulses to automobiles, hotels, and enterprise software.

What Investors Should Watch

The Tata Sons annual general meeting is scheduled for August 18, just six days away. The board will need to address succession planning under the shadow of Chandrasekaran's departure, with analysts watching whether Noel Tata — who took over as Tata Trusts chairman following Ratan Tata's death — will push for a candidate aligned with the trusts' vision.

For investors with exposure to Tata stocks, the key question is whether the leadership transition will stall or accelerate strategic decisions on Air India's restructuring, TCS's AI-driven growth strategy, and the long-debated listing of Tata Sons itself. Chandrasekaran's exit removes one side of the dispute, but the structural tension between commercial ambitions and philanthropic governance remains embedded in the conglomerate's DNA.
